title: Ransomware, Backups & Reporting
summary: What ransomware does, how backups save the day, and how to report an incident.

lessons.title: What is ransomware?
points: Ransomware is malware that encrypts files and systems, then demands payment to unlock them.
Many gangs also steal data first and threaten to publish it ("double extortion").
Common ways in: phishing, stolen passwords for remote access, and unpatched internet-facing systems.

lessons.title: Backups: the 3-2-1 rule
points: Keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy off-site.
Keep at least one backup offline or immutable so ransomware can't encrypt it too.
Test restores regularly. A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan.

lessons.title: Spot the warning signs
points: Files suddenly renamed with strange extensions or that won't open.
A ransom note on screen or in folders.
Your computer running very slowly, security tools disabled, or accounts you don't recognise.

lessons.title: Report it, fast
points: Disconnect from the network (unplug the cable or turn off Wi-Fi) but don't switch the device off unless told to. Memory can hold evidence.
Report to your IT/security team immediately with what you saw and when.
Don't try to pay, negotiate or 'clean it up' yourself. Security teams and authorities discourage paying ransoms.
lessons.tip: You are a sensor. Early reports turn disasters into minor incidents.

options: Encrypts files and demands payment, sometimes after stealing data
questions.why: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment. Many groups also steal data to threaten a leak.

questions.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule mean?
options: Back up 3 times a day for 2 weeks
questions.why: Three copies, on two different media, with one stored off-site, so a single event can't wipe them all.

questions.q: A backup that has never been test-restored can be fully relied on.
questions.why: Backups fail silently. Regular restore tests prove you can actually recover.

questions.q: Your files suddenly have a strange new extension and a note demands Bitcoin. What's your first step?
options: Pay quickly before the price rises
Disconnect from the network and report to IT/security
questions.why: Isolating the device helps stop spread, and immediate reporting lets responders act. Leave it powered on unless told otherwise.

questions.q: Keeping one backup offline or immutable helps protect it from ransomware.
questions.why: Ransomware often targets connected backups. An offline or immutable copy can't be encrypted by the attacker.

questions.q: Which is a common way ransomware gets into an organisation?
options: Phishing emails and stolen remote-access passwords
questions.why: Phishing, compromised credentials and unpatched internet-facing systems are among the most common entry points.

questions.q: If you think you caused an incident, you should wait until you're sure before reporting it.
questions.why: Report as soon as you suspect something. Minutes matter, and security teams would rather check a false alarm.

questions.q: What does 'double extortion' mean in ransomware?
options: Encrypting data and threatening to leak stolen copies
questions.why: Attackers steal data before encrypting, then threaten publication to increase pressure even if you have backups.

questions.q: What information is most useful when reporting a suspected incident?
options: What you saw, when it happened, what you clicked or opened, and which device/account
questions.why: Clear facts and timing help responders act quickly and accurately.

questions.q: Government cyber agencies such as CISA and the FBI generally discourage paying ransoms.
questions.why: Paying doesn't guarantee recovery and funds further attacks. Organisations should report incidents and seek guidance.
